newsitem.title: TANZANIA: IMF says Tanzania to implement VAT from July 1998.
newsitem.headline: IMF says Tanzania to implement VAT from July 1998.

text.p: Tanzania will postpone by six months implementation of value added tax (VAT) due to have taken effect on January 1 next year, the IMF said on Thursday.
International Monetary Fund (IMF) representative in Tanzania Festus Osunsade said VAT would now be implemented from July 1, 1998. He blamed the delay on technical grounds.
Diplomats said more time was required to prepare Tanzanians for the tax to avoid protests that followed its introduction in Ghana and Uganda or taxes duplication in neighbouring Kenya.
"It was a widely-shared view (among the government and donor community) that it would be more prudent for VAT implementation to start in July (1998)," Osunsade told Reuters.
He said implementation required massive data and computer back-up beyond the resources of the Tanzanian government which had requested funding assistance from the European Union (EU).
The EU agreed to the request covering supply and training in a package worth $15 million, but is bound by its own rules to place the bid for open tender among EU members.
Diplomats said that procedure was unlikely to be completed before November. Osunsade said Tanzania could use the extra time to educate the public and business community about the tax.

"The government wants to be fully prepared before launching VAT and avoid the bad experiences encountered by Uganda and Ghana," he said, adding adoption of the complex VAT required caution and should not be hastily implemented by Tanzania.
A 17 percent VAT was launched in Uganda in 1996 without wide consultation with the business community. Shops and businesses closed in protest. Teething problems have since been ironed out.
Similar problems were reported in Ghana which introduced a 20 percent VAT without an effective education campaign.
Financial analysts said Kenya's 15 percent VAT did not work well because there remained considerable tax duplication.
"It works well when it replaces all other taxes. In Kenya there is still a tax on petroleum, newsprint and alcohol and paperwork is doubled for tax payers," said one senior analyst.

VAT is seen as a key element in simplifying Tanzania's tax regime, sharply criticised by businessmen and investors as inequitable and too bureacratic. Finance Minister Daniel Yona has pledged a new "tax-payer-friendly" regime when he presents his state budget in June.
The semi-autonomous Zanzibar islands, a union partner with mainland Tanzania, are even less prepared for VAT.
"Zanzibar will be coming on board with the same timetable and is even less prepared. This will allow more time for them to be fully-integrated into the VAT programme," Osunsade said.

Agreement on VAT by Zanzibar and the mainland is vital in achieving tax harmonisation to close the "Zanzibar route", in which the government previously lost millions of dollars in revenue to traders exploiting lower import tariffs in Zanzibar.
